clue.text: Promoter refers to queen accepting one

indicators.note: something accepting another thing takes it in, so the pair of words around it hold the numeral

parts.note: to advert to a matter is to refer to it, so 'refers to' gives adverts
I is the Roman numeral for one
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the standard abbreviation for the Queen

explanation.surface: A publicist mentions the monarch taking someone on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refers to' reads as a verb phrase about a promoter, but it is one unit: to advert to something is an old way of saying refer to it.
explanation.definitionFit: An advertiser pushes a product, so is a promoter of it.

clue.text: Feel sleepy — right to duck out of it

indicators.note: the letter for right is put to, that is into, the word for duck, the plunge from which it must emerge

parts.note: to dowse (or douse) is to duck or plunge into water

explanation.surface: Someone nodding off has the right to get out of a ducking.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside DOWSE after its D; 'out of it' adds to the sleepy picture, since a drowsy person is out of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To drowse is to doze or be half asleep.

clue.text: Warehouse being erected, bold in style

indicators.note: in a down clue something erected is stood upright, so the letters read from the bottom up
the word for bold sits in the word for style

parts.note: tone is manner or style, as in the tone of a piece
pert means saucy or bold

explanation.surface: A storehouse is going up, built in a showy style.
explanation.walkthrough: The container makes TOPERTNE, which 'being erected' turns upright; an entrepot is a port where goods are stored for re-export.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrepot is a trading depot or storage centre for goods in transit.

clue.text: Standard test on product, interrupted by a cry of annoyance

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are broken into by the exclamation
a product is something made or worked up, so the words test and on are worked into a new order

parts.note: ouch is an exclamation of pain or annoyance

explanation.surface: A benchmark trial of some merchandise is disrupted by someone exclaiming in irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Product' turns TEST ON into TSTONE, and 'interrupted by' puts OUCH after its first T. 'Standard test' looks like the definition, but 'test' is part of the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A touchstone is a criterion or benchmark against which things are judged.

clue.text: Staff shows unusual respect it's different in America!

indicators.note: unusual signals the letters of the next word set out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A rod of office displays odd deference, and Americans spell it otherwise.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail is a comment: Americans spell the word -ER at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceptre is the ceremonial rod or staff a monarch holds.

clue.text: Increase the size of several choirs, say

definitions.meaning: to ... a hole is to widen it with a tool

explanation.definitionFit: Reaming enlarges a bore, and a ream is a paper quantity of many quires.

clue.text: College steward put broken clip in hair

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go in the word for hair

parts.note: a mane is a long head of hair

indicators.note: broken signals that the word clip is smashed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone pushes a snapped hairclip into their locks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' gives CIPL. A manciple is a historical college office, also one of Chaucer's pilgrims in The Canterbury Tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A manciple is the officer who buys provisions for an Oxford or Cambridge college or Inn of Court.

clue.text: Bishop has sexy photo! It takes the biscuit!

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
randy means lustful or sexy
a snap is a snapshot photograph

explanation.surface: A clergyman with a racy picture is the limit, it really takes the biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the biscuit' is British for being the outrageous limit; here the answer literally is the biscuit. A brandy snap is a thin rolled ginger biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy snap is a crisp, curled gingerbread wafer, a kind of cookie.

clue.text: Cake a girl made back to front?

indicators.note: the letter at the back of the girl's name is brought round to the front

parts.note: Claire is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Did a girl bake a pastry the wrong way round?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made back to front' moves the final E of CLAIRE to the start.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclair is a long choux pastry filled with cream and iced with chocolate.

clue.text: Voluntary employment of an indecent nature, say

parts.note: a post is a job or position of employment

indicators.note: say signals that the word for indecent is taken only as heard

parts.note: lewd means obscene or indecent

explanation.surface: Unpaid work of a smutty kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Voluntary' is the noun: an organ piece. A postlude is the voluntary played at the end of a service.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ voluntary closing a church service is called a postlude.

clue.text: Emergency rations for male Muscovite in prison

indicators.note: the man and the mineral go in the word for prison

parts.note: pen is slang for a prison, short for penitentiary
muscovite is a common form of the mineral mica

explanation.surface: Survival food for a Russian man behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muscovite' looks like a Russian from Moscow, but here it is the mineral mica.
explanation.definitionFit: Pemmican is dried pounded meat mixed with fat, carried as compact survival food.

clue.text: Harvest in Korea, perhaps

indicators.note: the answer lies in the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: Gathering crops in the Korean peninsula.
explanation.definitionFit: To reap is to cut and gather a crop.

clue.text: Crude game leads to disorderly behaviour

parts.note: rough means crude or unrefined
house, or housey-housey, is an old name for the game of bingo

explanation.surface: An unrefined pastime ends in rowdy conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: HOUSE is the British army and fairground name for bingo.
explanation.definitionFit: Roughhouse is boisterous, brawling horseplay.

clue.text: Pretty sash designed for the dance

indicators.note: designed means worked into a new pattern, so the two words' letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: A lovely sash made specially for the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: A strathspey is a slow Scottish country dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A strathspey is a Scottish reel-like step, slower than a reel.

clue.text: Competition for East End university's inside decoration

indicators.note: End points to the last letter of the word East
the university letter goes inside the word for decoration

parts.note: an ornament is a decoration
U is the abbreviation for university, and 's is read as is

explanation.surface: A contest for London's East End, with ornament at a college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East End' is London's cockney district on the surface, but gives only the end of 'East'. 'Inside' puts U into ORNAMENT after its O.
explanation.definitionFit: A tournament is a sporting contest with many entrants.

clue.text: Soothing words when Head leaves meeting-place

indicators.note: the head, the first letter, departs from the word for a meeting-place

parts.note: a junction is where roads or railways meet

explanation.surface: Comforting speech as the headteacher departs a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like a headteacher, but it is the first letter, J, of JUNCTION.
explanation.definitionFit: Unction is an oily, soothing manner of speech, a sense taken from anointing.

clue.text: Punishes prisoner, being above the limit

indicators.note: in a down entry one word placed above another comes first

parts.note: a con is a convict, a prisoner
to fine is to punish with a money penalty

explanation.surface: Penalising an inmate for going over the limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The limit' is singular while the answer is a plural noun meaning boundaries; the setter leans on the sense of an outer limit.
explanation.definitionFit: Confines are boundaries, the edge or limit of something.

clue.text: Boy restrains impulse to become a ship's doctor

indicators.note: the word for boy holds back, so contains, the word for impulse

parts.note: a son is a boy
an urge is a sudden impulse

explanation.surface: A lad curbs his desires to go to sea as a medic.
explanation.definitionFit: The medical officer on a ship has long been called the ship's surgeon.

clue.text: Game involving double-header is hard for a swimmer

indicators.note: involving means wrapped around, so the game holds the letter

parts.note: golf is a game
the header, the first letter, of double
taken as written
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A sports fixture played twice in a day is tough on a swimmer.
explanation.walkthrough: A double-header is two games played back to back, but here it is the first letter of 'double'. 'Involving' puts D inside GOLF.
explanation.definitionFit: A goldfish is a small orange freshwater fish kept as a pet.

clue.text: A vast number laid up in old Jerusalem

indicators.note: the word for sick goes in the old name for the holy city

parts.note: Zion is the biblical name for Jerusalem
laid up means confined to bed, ill

explanation.surface: A great many were bedridden in ancient Jerusalem.
explanation.walkthrough: Zion was originally a hill in Jerusalem, and its name came to stand for the whole city.
explanation.definitionFit: A zillion is an informal word for an indefinitely huge quantity.

clue.text: Like George I, employing singular German in preference to Scot

parts.note: Hans is a typical German name; jokingly taken as a plural, its singular drops the S
choosing one thing over another is preferring it
Ian is a typical Scottish first name

explanation.surface: Like George I, who used a lone German rather than a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: The humour is treating HANS as a plural so a single German is HAN. George I came from Hanover, founding the Hanoverian line of British kings.
explanation.definitionFit: George I was the first British monarch from the House of Hanover.

clue.text: US city representative providing illumination

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
an MP, a Member of Parliament, is an elected representative

explanation.surface: A politician from Los Angeles sheds light.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamp is a source of light, standing here for the light itself.

clue.text: Falcon at Camelot, useful for a spell?

definitions.text: at Camelot, useful for a spell?
definitions.meaning: the wizard of King Arthur's court, a caster of spells

explanation.definitionFit: A merlin is a small bird of prey, and Arthurian legend's magician shares the name.

clue.text: Poor relation from Indo-China

indicators.note: poor signals the word relation in a bad state, its letters disordered

explanation.surface: A needy relative from Southeast Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor relation' reads as a phrase, but 'Poor' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriental describes the East, including Indochina.

clue.text: Pour down the side, by the sound of it

indicators.note: the phrase says the word for side is taken as heard, not as written

parts.note: a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: Rain lashes down the flank of something, judging by the noise.
explanation.definitionFit: When rain teems it falls in torrents.

clue.text: Unbelievable, King Charles leaving such food

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; 'such food' is food so described

indicators.note: the king's letters depart from the word for unbelievable

parts.note: incredible means unbelievable
CR, Carolus Rex, is King Charles's royal cipher

explanation.surface: Amazingly, King Charles walked out on such fare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Such food' points back to the wordplay's result: food that cannot be eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Food unfit to eat is described as inedible.

clue.text: Receive article which makes us foam at the mouth

parts.note: to see a visitor is to receive them
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: Getting a newspaper piece that makes us furious.
explanation.definitionFit: To seethe is to rage inwardly, like boiling water.

clue.text: Tiny writing, produced by a horologist

parts.note: minute means very small
hand is handwriting

explanation.surface: Small handwriting turned out by a clockmaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the answer as a clockmaker's product.
explanation.definitionFit: A horologist makes clocks, which have a long pointer for the minutes.
